Anthropic is endorsing California State Senator Scott Wiener’s SB 53. This bill provides a strong foundation to govern powerful AI systems built by frontier AI companies like ours, and does so via transparency rather than technical micromanagement.Frontier AI safety is best addressed at the federal level, and we prefer a strong nationwide standard to a patchwork of state regulations. But federal action remains uncertain, and powerful AI advancements won’t wait for consensus in Washington.We commend Senator Wiener and Governor Newsom for their leadership on responsible AI governance. The question is whether we develop AI governance thoughtfully today, or reactively tomorrow. SB 53 offers a solid path toward the former. We encourage California to pass it.https://lnkd.in/e2x22v3Q

New Anthropic research: together with theAI Security Instituteand the Alan Turing Institute, we found that just a few malicious documents can produce vulnerabilities in AI models—regardless of the size of the model or its training data.Previous research suggested that attackers might need to poison a percentage of an AI model’s training data to produce a backdoor. Our results challenge this—we find that even a small, fixed number of documents can poison an LLM of any size.Our findings suggest that data-poisoning attacks might be more practical than previously believed.Read more:https://lnkd.in/dMwWXeaM

New Anthropic research: How university students use Claude.We ran a privacy-preserving analysis of a million education-related conversations to produce our first Education Report.Our findings show students primarily use Claude to create and improve educational content (39.3%) and provide technical explanations (33.5%).Computer Science dominates AI usage, representing 38.6% of Claude conversations despite making up only 5.4% of US degrees.We created a taxonomy for how students interact with AI, and tracked how common those interaction styles were across different subjects. Science and Math saw more Collaborative Problem Solving; Education saw more Direct Output Creation.Our taxonomy reveals distinct interaction patterns: more Collaborative Problem Solving in Science/Math and Direct Output Creation in Education fields.We also wondered, are students using AI to cheat?It’s hard to know whether any specific category is cheating or legitimate study, but we did notice some concerning patterns: students straightforwardly asking for answers, or asking Claude to rewrite an essay to avoid plagiarism detection.Students mostly used AI to create and analyze, according to our analysis using Bloom’s Taxonomy of educational goals.Whether cheating or not, this raises important questions about how to stop students offloading important cognitive tasks to AI. AI can empower learning in remarkable ways. But we’re under no illusions that all the changes it’s bringing to education are positive.Our research will help educators and policymakers ensure that AI deepens, rather than undermines, learning.Read the full report:https://lnkd.in/eABqfPtaWe’re working with universities to help realize the benefits of AI.
